title: Śalkair agnim: crossing beyond death
theme: The speaker, kindling the fire with wood, asks to win both worlds and, having won them, says: I cross beyond death. It ends the six verses on death.

words.context: The commentator glosses it as dry sticks, in the form of kindling.
The commentator: the āhavanīya and the other ritual fires.

words.gram: present participle middle, m. nom. sg.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «लोकाविहपरलक्षणौ सनें प्राप्नुयां त्वदनुग्रहात्» — the two worlds, this one and the next: may I win them by your grace

words.role: main verb of the first line
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «सनें प्राप्नुयां» — may I obtain
The anonymous commentator: by a change of case it stands for the accusative: «व्यत्ययेनोभौ लोकावृद्ध्वा लब्ध्वा» — having gained both worlds

words.role: main verb of the second line
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «मृत्युमहमतितराम्यमृतो भवामि» — I cross beyond death, I become deathless

sandhi.type: visarga after ai before a vowel; -aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: The visarga of śalkaiḥ becomes r before a vowel; indhānaḥ + ubhau → indhāna ubhau, the visarga dropped (P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य)).
sanem + aham → sanem aham, written together.

sandhi.type: visarga after o before a voiced sound; ā + a → ā
sandhi.rule: The visargas of ubhayoḥ and lokayoḥ become r before l and ṛ; ṛdhvā + ati → ṛdhvāti, the avagraha marking the merged a (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)).

morphology.note: A Vedic optative first person singular of √san ‘to win’; the commentator, as printed, writes सनें and glosses prāpnuyām.
A Vedic gerund of √ṛdh. The base and the Tirupati e-text write ऋध्वा; the Ānandāśrama text writes ऋद्ध्वा (corrections.json, a witness error), the spelling the commentator also uses (ऋद्ध्वा).
With ati, separated from it by mṛtyum (tmesis): ati-tarāmi, ‘I cross beyond’.

translation.literal: Kindling the fire with chips of wood, may I win both worlds. Having prospered in both worlds, I cross beyond death.
translation.readable: Kindling the fire with dry sticks, may I gain both this world and the next; and having gained them both, I pass beyond death.

anvaya: अहम् शल्कैः अग्निम् इन्धानः उभौ लोकौ सनेम् । अहम् उभयोः लोकयोः ऋध्वा मृत्युम् अति तरामि ।
syntax: A wish in the optative (sanem) whose subject is described by a participle (indhānaḥ) with its instrumental and object; then a statement in the present (ati … tarāmi) preceded by a gerund (ṛdhvā).

ambiguities.note: Locative ‘in both worlds’ (prospering in both); the commentator reads it, by a change of case, as an accusative object of ṛdhvā: ‘having gained both worlds’.
The commentator explains it as enjoying this world’s goods for a full life and at its end becoming a god («यावदायुरैहिकान्भोगान्भुक्त्वाऽन्ते देवो भवामीत्यभिप्रायः»), not as liberation.

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: One anuṣṭubh verse printed in two lines; the checker counts 15 and 15 syllables, the first and last pādas a syllable short as written (indhāna ubhau is kept in hiatus, and ṛdhvā ’ti merges the a of ati).

beginner: This short verse closes the group of six verses about turning death away. It pictures the speaker at the ritual fire, feeding it with chips of dry wood. While kindling it, the speaker asks to gain both worlds, this one and the next. The second line then says, in the present tense: having prospered in both worlds, I cross beyond death. The old commentator explains that this shows how good action bears fruit in both worlds. He reads crossing beyond death as living out a full life, enjoying the good things of this world, and at its end becoming a god. He does not take it here as liberation.
analogy: Like tending a small fire through the night until the dawn comes.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the speaker, kindling the fire, asks to win both worlds, and having prospered in both, crosses beyond death.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read it?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: the speaker asks this of the Lord; it shows that good action bears fruit in both worlds («एतेन लोकद्वयं सत्कर्मणा फलतीत्युक्तं भवति»), and crossing death means becoming deathless («मृत्युमहमतितराम्यमृतो भवामि»), which he explains as a full life and then the state of a god.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this verse is in the edition’s sources. Only the anonymous commentator comments on it, and his reading is a prayer to the Lord (paramātman) without a school argument; Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s files contain no comment on this verse, and Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among the sources.

contemporary.text: The verse sets its largest hope, passing beyond death, beside a small daily act: feeding a fire with sticks. Large hopes are often carried by small and repeated actions. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What small thing do you do every day that matters to you?
reflect.deeper: Why might the commentator read ‘crossing death’ here as a full life rather than as liberation?
reflect.practice: Choose one small task you will do carefully each day this week.

references.text: Only the anonymous commentator comments on this anuvāka; the edition’s Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara files have no comment on it (the concordance maps are empty here, correctly).

flags.note: The Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text reads ऋद्ध्वा (corrections.json, a witness error); the base and the Tirupati e-text read ऋध्वा. The anonymous commentator’s gloss uses ऋद्ध्वा.
The commentator’s gloss on śalkaiḥ is printed «सप्निद्रूपैः», apparently a misprint (perhaps for samid-, kindling); the word table paraphrases it.
